A small bead is guided around a fixed horizontal circular track. In a first run it moves at a constant angular speed \(3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). (a) [3]

Find the radius of the track.

(b) [2]

Find the distance travelled in 8 seconds during the second run.
original.hint_html: Compare the radial accelerations before finding the linear speed.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

For each steady run the radial acceleration is \(r\omega^2\). The same radius is used in both runs, so \[25r-9r=12.\] Thus \(16r=12\) and \(r=3/4\ \mathrm m\).

Part (b)

The speed is \(v=r\omega=(3/4)5=15/4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It is constant during the run, so the distance is \((15/4)8=30\ \mathrm m\).

Find the speed of the particle and state the direction of the resultant force.
original.hint_html: Use the mass and radius as well as the force.

For the inner particle, tension acts outwards but limiting friction acts inwards. Hence \[\frac14mg-T=ma\frac{g}{5a}=\frac15mg.\] It follows that \(T=mg/20\), which is positive.

(a) [6]

original.hint_html: Use a cosine variable constrained to lie between zero and one.

Part (a)

Let \(c=\cos\theta=(a-h)/a\), where \(\theta\) is the angle of the normal reaction to the upward vertical. original.stem_html: A particle moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle on the smooth inside of a fixed hemispherical bowl of radius \(a\). original.question_html:
A particle moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle on the smooth inside of a fixed hemispherical bowl of radius \(a\). Its height above the lowest point is \(h\), and its angular speed is \(\omega\). In a second steady motion the angular speed is \(\sqrt2\,\omega\) and the height is \(3h\). Both orbits lie below the rim.

(a) [3]

Show that \(\omega^2=g/(a-h)\).

(b) [4]

Find \(h\), and state the normal reaction in the second motion for a particle of mass \(m\).
original.hint_html: The square of the angular-speed multiplier is 2, not √2.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let the normal reaction make angle \(\theta\) with the upward vertical. Its equations are \[N\cos\theta=mg,\qquad N\sin\theta=m\omega^2a\sin\theta.\] Eliminating \(N\) gives \(\omega^2=g/(a\cos\theta)\). Since \(a\cos\theta=a-h\), the required result follows.

Part (b)

The second motion satisfies \(2\omega^2=g/(a-3h)\). Combining with (a), \[\frac2{a-h}=\frac1{a-3h},\qquad 2a-6h=a-h.\] Thus \(h=a/5\); the second height \(3a/5\) is indeed below the rim. In that motion \(\cos\theta_2=1-3/5=2/5\), so \(N_2=mg/(2/5)=5mg/2\).

Find the tension in \(AP\).
original.hint_html: The two tensions need not be equal: the two strings are separate.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Equal string lengths put \(P\) halfway between the heights of \(A\) and \(B\). Each vertical separation is \(3l/5\), and the circle radius is \(4l/5\). Thus \[\frac35(T_A-T_B)=mg,\qquad \frac45(T_A+T_B)=m\omega^2\frac{4l}{5}.\] Hence \(T_A-T_B=5mg/3\), while \(T_A+T_B=ml\omega^2\). Adding yields the stated \(T_A\). (b) [3]

(c) [2]

Find the angle \(\beta\) that \(PQ\) makes with the downward vertical.
original.hint_html: Add the equations of the two particles to remove the force in the lower string.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

For \(OP\), \(\sin\alpha=3/5\) and \(\cos\alpha=4/5\). The upper string supports the weights of both particles: the vertical components of the force in \(PQ\) cancel when their two vertical equations are added. Hence \(T_1(4/5)=3mg\), giving \(T_1=15mg/4\).

Part (b)

Adding the two horizontal inward equations cancels the internal force from \(PQ\). The total required inward force is \((2m)(3a)\omega^2+m(6a)\omega^2=12ma\omega^2\). Therefore \[\frac{15mg}{4}\frac35=12ma\omega^2,\] which gives \(\omega^2=3g/(16a)\).

Part (c)

For \(Q\) alone, \(T_2\cos\beta=mg\) and \(T_2\sin\beta=m(6a)\omega^2\). Dividing gives \(\tan\beta=6a\omega^2/g=9/8\). The acute angle is selected by the stated geometry.

It is projected vertically downwards from \(A=(-a,0)\) with speed \(u\), passes through the lowest point and ascends on the right. Let \(B\) be the point on this ascent with \(y=ka\), where \(0\lt k\lt 1\).

(a) [4]

In one experiment \(u^2=8ag/5\), and the reaction at B is one quarter of the reaction at A. Find k.

(b) [3]

For this value of k, find the least launch speed that allows the particle to reach B without losing contact before B.

(c) [3]

At this least launch speed the particle leaves the surface at B. Find its greatest height above O during the ensuing free flight.
original.hint_html: Use energy and the nonnegative normal reaction together. After release, switch to projectile equations.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Energy between \(A\) and \(B\) gives \(v_B^2=u^2-2gka\). At \(A\), gravity has no radial component, so \(N_A=mu^2/a\). At \(B\), the inward component of weight is \(mgk\), giving \[N_B=\frac{mv_B^2}{a}-mgk=\frac{mu^2}{a}-3mgk.\] Thus \(8/5-3k=(1/4)(8/5)\), so \(k=2/5\).

Part (b)

While contact is maintained, \(N/(mg)=u^2/(ag)-3y/a\). On the upper ascent this is smallest at \(B\), so nonnegative reaction up to \(B\) requires \(u^2/(ag)\ge3k=6/5\). Equality gives the least speed. At \(B\), \(v_B^2=agk=2ag/5\gt 0\). Merely requiring \(v_B^2\ge0\) would give too small a launch speed.

Part (c)

At release, \(\cos\theta=k=2/5\), \(v_B^2=2ag/5\), and the upward component of velocity is \(v_B\sin\theta\). Its square is \((2ag/5)(21/25)=42ag/125\). The additional rise is this quantity divided by \(2g\), namely \(21a/125\). Add the release height \(2a/5\) to get \(71a/125\). The apex occurs before recontact with the shell.

Starting at \((-a,0)\), relative to horizontal and upward axes through \(O\), it is projected vertically downwards with speed \(\sqrt{12ag/5}\). It passes through the lowest point and ascends on the right before losing contact.

It passes through the lowest point and ascends on the right before losing contact.

(a) [3]

Find the cosine of the angle to the upward vertical at loss of contact.

(b) [5]

Find the height above O when the particle first crosses the vertical through O after release, and state whether it is then rising or falling.
original.hint_html: Write separate horizontal and vertical equations from the release point.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

At a height \(ac\), energy gives \(v^2/(ag)=12/5-2c\). The reaction is \(N/(mg)=12/5-3c\). Setting \(N=0\) gives \(c=4/5\), with positive release speed \(v=\sqrt{4ag/5}\).

At release, \((x,y)=(3a/5,4a/5)\). The velocity points up and left, with components \(-4v/5\) and \(3v/5\). Horizontal motion gives elapsed time \[t=\frac{3a}{4v}=\frac{3\sqrt5}{8}\sqrt{\frac ag}.\] The vertical position is \(y=4a/5+(3v/5)t-gt^2/2\). Here \((3v/5)t=9a/20\) and \(gt^2/2=45a/128\), so \(y=115a/128\). At this time the vertical velocity is \((6\sqrt5/25-3\sqrt5/8)\sqrt{ag}=-27\sqrt5\sqrt{ag}/200\lt 0\). The particle is falling. The axis-crossing point is inside the cylinder; the first positive recontact time is \((24\sqrt5/25)\sqrt{a/g}\), which is later.

original.stem_html: A fixed smooth solid sphere of radius \(a\) rests on horizontal ground. A particle of mass \(m\) is launched horizontally from the top with speed \(u\). It follows the outer surface and leaves it where the radius makes angle \(\theta\) with the upward vertical. After leaving, it moves freely under gravity.
original.question_html:
A fixed smooth solid sphere of radius \(a\) rests on horizontal ground. A particle of mass \(m\) is launched horizontally from the top with speed \(u\). It follows the outer surface and leaves it where the radius makes angle \(\theta\) with the upward vertical. After leaving, it moves freely under gravity.

(a) [3]

Show that \(\cos\theta=(u^2+2ag)/(3ag)\).

(b) [3]

Given that \(\cos\theta=3/4\), find the vertical velocity just before ground impact.

(c) [3]

Find the elapsed time between leaving the sphere and ground impact.
original.hint_html: Use downward velocity signs consistently; the release point is above the centre, not above ground by only a cosθ.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(\cos\theta=(u^2+2ag)/(3ag)\).

(b)

\(\displaystyle-\frac{7\sqrt5}{8}\sqrt{ag}\), taking upwards as positive.

(c)

\(\displaystyle t=\frac{7\sqrt5-\sqrt{21}}8\sqrt{\frac ag}\approx1.38\sqrt{\frac ag}\).
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

At angle \(\theta\), energy gives \(v^2=u^2+2ag(1-\cos\theta)\). On the outside, the normal force acts outwards, so \(mg\cos\theta-N=mv^2/a\). At loss of contact \(N=0\); substitute \(v^2=ag\cos\theta\) into energy and rearrange to obtain the stated result.

Part (b)

The release speed squared is \(3ag/4\), and \(\sin^2\theta=7/16\). The release vertical velocity is downward, with square \(21ag/64\). The release height above the ground is \(a(1+3/4)=7a/4\). Thus the impact vertical speed squared is \(21ag/64+2g(7a/4)=245ag/64\). The signed velocity is \(-7\sqrt5\sqrt{ag}/8\).

Part (c)

The vertical release velocity is \(-\sqrt{21}\sqrt{ag}/8\). Since \(v_y=v_{y0}-gt\), \[-\frac{7\sqrt5}{8}\sqrt{ag}=-\frac{\sqrt{21}}8\sqrt{ag}-gt.\] Therefore \(t=(7\sqrt5-\sqrt{21})\sqrt{a/g}/8\). It is positive. Part (a) also gives \(u^2=ag/4\lt ag\), so initial contact at the top is physically possible.

original.stem_html: A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). original.question_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). It starts at a horizontal level with \(O\) and is projected vertically downwards with speed \(\sqrt{3ag/5}\). After passing the bottom it reaches a point \(Q\) on the lower ascending arc, where the string makes acute angle \(\theta\) with the downward vertical. At \(Q\), its speed is \(\sqrt{kag}\) and its tension is \(12mg/5\). It is then deliberately detached from the string.

(a) [4]

Find \(k\) and \(\cos\theta\).

(b) [4]

Find the greatest height above the lowest point reached during the subsequent free flight.
original.hint_html: The particle is ascending even though it is still below the centre.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\). The point \(Q\) is \(ac\) below the starting level, so energy gives \(k=3/5+2c\). The radial equation at the lower point is \(12mg/5-mgc=mkg\), or \(k+c=12/5\). Combining gives \(3/5+3c=12/5\), so \(c=3/5\) and \(k=9/5\).

Part (b)

At release, \(Q\) is \(a(1-3/5)=2a/5\) above the lowest point. Its upward tangential component is \(v\sin\theta\), with square \((9ag/5)(16/25)=144ag/125\). The additional rise is \(72a/125\). Therefore the greatest height above the lowest point is \[\frac25a+\frac{72}{125}a=\frac{122}{125}a.\] This is slightly below the horizontal level through \(O\). The release is imposed deliberately; it does not occur because the tension is zero.

original.stem_html: A particle moves on the smooth inner surface of a fixed circular cylinder of radius \(a\), in a vertical cross-section with centre \(O\). original.question_html:
A particle moves on the smooth inner surface of a fixed circular cylinder of radius \(a\), in a vertical cross-section with centre \(O\). It is projected to the right from the lowest point with speed \(\sqrt{19ag/5}\). After losing contact on the upper right, it moves freely until it next meets the cylinder. Use horizontal and upward coordinates relative to \(O\).

(a) [3]

Find the cosine of the angle to the upward vertical at loss of contact.

(b) [5]

Find the next contact point and the elapsed time from release to that contact.

(c) [2]

Explain why this is the first contact after release.
original.hint_html: After release solve for the next intersection with the entire circle; do not assume it is the bottom.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The bottom-to-point rise is \(a(1+c)\), with \(c\) the upward cosine. Thus \(v^2/(ag)=19/5-2(1+c)=9/5-2c\). At zero reaction \(v^2=agc\), giving \(c=3/5\). The release coordinates are \((4a/5,3a/5)\).

Part (b)

At release \(v=\sqrt{3ag/5}\), directed up and left. Write \(X=x/a\), \(Y=y/a\) and \(\tau=t\sqrt{g/a}\). The free-flight equations are \[X=\frac45-\frac{3\sqrt{15}}{25}\tau,\qquad Y=\frac35+\frac{4\sqrt{15}}{25}\tau-\frac12\tau^2.\] Substitute these into the cylinder equation \(X^2+Y^2=1\). Expansion and factorisation give \[X^2+Y^2-1=\tau^3\left(\frac{\tau}{4}-\frac{4\sqrt{15}}{25}\right).\] The positive root is \(\tau=16\sqrt{15}/25\). Substitution gives \(X=-44/125\), \(Y=-117/125\). Restore dimensions for the time and coordinates.

Part (c)

In the factorisation above, \(\tau^3\gt 0\) for positive time and the bracket is negative until the stated positive root. Hence the whole preceding flight lies strictly inside the circle. There is no earlier positive intersection. Also \(44^2+117^2=125^2\), confirming the final point lies on the surface.

In a vertical section of a fixed smooth spherical shell of radius \(a\) and centre \(O\), let \(A=(-4a/5,-3a/5)\), \(C=(0,-a)\) and \(B=(4a/5,3a/5)\). A particle of mass \(m\) is projected tangentially from \(A\), initially moving towards \(C\), with speed \(u\). The normal reactions at \(A\) and \(C\) are in the ratio \(11:15\).

(a) [4]

Find \(u^2\) in terms of \(a\) and \(g\).

(b) [5]

Determine whether the particle reaches B while remaining in contact with the surface.

(c) [3]

Find the greatest reaction before contact is lost and the speed at loss of contact.
original.hint_html: An inner surface requires a nonnegative inward reaction. Check it before using a later point.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(u^2=27ag/10\).

(b)

No. Contact is lost first at height \(a/2\) above \(O\).

(c)

\(N_{\max}=9mg/2\), \(v_{\rm loss}=\sqrt{ag/2}\).
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The fall from \(A\) to \(C\) is \(2a/5\), so \(v_C^2=u^2+4ag/5\). The inward component of weight at \(A\) is \(-3mg/5\), hence \(N_A=mu^2/a+3mg/5\). At the bottom, \(N_C=mv_C^2/a+mg=mu^2/a+9mg/5\). Writing \(q=u^2/(ag)\), the ratio gives \(15(q+3/5)=11(q+9/5)\). Thus \(4q=54/5\), and \(q=27/10\).

Part (b)

For any point at height \(y=ca\), energy gives \[\frac{v^2}{ag}=\frac{27}{10}+2\left(-\frac35-c\right)=\frac32-2c.\] The inward radial equation gives \(N/(mg)=3/2-3c\). The first zero on the upper ascent is at \(c=1/2\), before the particle reaches the height \(3a/5\) of \(B\). At that zero the speed squared is \(ag/2\gt 0\). At \(B\), energy alone would predict \(v_B^2=3ag/10\gt 0\), but the contact formula would require \(N_B=-3mg/10\). An inner surface cannot pull the particle outwards, so this is not a physically possible continuation in contact.

Part (c)

The expression \(N/(mg)=3/2-3c\) is greatest at the lowest point \(c=-1\), which lies on the actual route. Hence \(N_{\max}=9mg/2\). At loss of contact \(c=1/2\), so \(v^2/(ag)=3/2-1=1/2\), giving \(v=\sqrt{ag/2}\).

original.title: A three-quarter turn before slackening
original.stem_html: A particle of mass \(m\) is joined to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Initially it is at \(A=(4a/5,3a/5)\), relative to horizontal and upward axes through \(O\). It is projected tangentially in the clockwise, initially downward, direction with speed \(u\). The string first becomes slack after the radius has turned clockwise through \(270^\circ\).
original.question_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is joined to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Initially it is at \(A=(4a/5,3a/5)\), relative to horizontal and upward axes through \(O\). It is projected tangentially in the clockwise, initially downward, direction with speed \(u\). The string first becomes slack after the radius has turned clockwise through \(270^\circ\).

(a) [5]

Find \(u^2\) in terms of \(a\) and \(g\).

(b) [4]

Find the greatest tension before slackening.
original.hint_html: Locate the endpoint of the 270° turn before writing the energy equation.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

A clockwise rotation through \(270^\circ\) is equivalent geometrically to an anticlockwise rotation through \(90^\circ\), so the release point is \(B=(-3a/5,4a/5)\). The rise from \(A\) to \(B\) is \(a/5\). Hence \(v_B^2=u^2-2ag/5\). At \(B\), zero tension gives \(v_B^2/a=g(4/5)\). Therefore \(u^2-2ag/5=4ag/5\), giving \(u^2=6ag/5\). A particle of mass \(m\) moves on the smooth inner surface of a spherical shell of radius \(a\) and centre \(O\), in one vertical plane. In a second experiment it starts at the lowest point with the same speed \(u\), and loses contact at upward radius-angle \(2\beta\). Both loss points are in the upper half of the circle, and \(0\lt \beta\lt \pi/4\).

(a) [5]

Show that the first experiment gives \(u^2=ag(\frac12+3\cos\beta)\).

(b) [5]

(c) [4]

Let \(c=\cos\beta\). The release height is \(ac\), so the gain in height from the first start is \(a(c+1/4)\). At release the normal force is zero, and the radial equation gives \(v^2=agc\). In the second experiment the height gained is \(a(1+\cos2\beta)\), and the release speed squared is \(ag\cos2\beta\). Hence \(u^2/(ag)=2+3\cos2\beta=6c^2-1\). Equating with (a) gives \(1/2+3c=6c^2-1\), or \(4c^2-2c-1=0\). Thus \(c=(1\pm\sqrt5)/4\). The negative root is impossible; the positive root is between \(\sqrt2/2\) and 1, as required by \(0\lt \beta\lt \pi/4\). (a) [3]

Find the speed and tension immediately before collision.

(b) [5]

Find all possible values of k.

(c) [3]

(a)

\(U=\sqrt{10ag}\), \(T_-=11mg\).

(b)

(c)

original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The fall to the bottom is \(a\), so \(U^2=8ag+2ag=10ag\). At the bottom the radial equation is \(T_--mg=mU^2/a\). Thus \(T_-=11mg\).

Let \(s=1+k\gt 1\). Momentum gives the common speed \(V=U/s\). The new tension is \[T_+=smg+\frac{smV^2}{a}=mg\left(s+\frac{10}{s}\right).\] The given ratio makes this equal to \(7mg\). Therefore \(s^2-7s+10=0\), so \(s=2\) or 5. Both exceed 1, giving \(k=1\) or 4. The coalescence reduces kinetic energy for both values.

Part (c)

A string-constrained complete circle needs bottom speed squared at least \(5ag\): energy removes \(4ag\) on reaching the top, where speed squared must still be at least \(ag\). Here \(V^2=10ag/s^2\), equal to \(5ag/2\) for \(s=2\) and \(2ag/5\) for \(s=5\). Both are below the threshold, so neither case gives complete circular motion.

original.question_html:
A particle \(P\) of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). It starts with the string horizontal and is projected vertically downwards with speed \(\sqrt{43ag}\). At the lowest point it collides directly and perfectly elastically with a stationary particle \(Q\) of mass \(km\). The particle \(P\) rebounds with just sufficient speed to complete a vertical circle in the limiting sense. No horizontal external impulse acts during the collision.

(a) [3]

Find the speed of P immediately before collision.

(b) [2]

Find the velocity of P immediately after collision, taking its incoming direction as positive.

(c) [3]

Find k.
original.hint_html: The limiting complete circle requires a nonzero speed at its highest point.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The loss of potential energy is \(mga\). Hence \(\frac12mU^2=\frac12m(43ag)+mga\), so \(U^2=45ag\) and \(U=3\sqrt{5ag}\).

Part (b)

At the limiting top point, tension is zero and \(v_{\rm top}^2=ag\). Energy from the bottom to the top requires bottom speed squared \(ag+4ag=5ag\). Rebound makes the signed velocity \(-\sqrt{5ag}\). Zero tension at the single top instant is the limiting full-circle case, not a claim of an extended slack phase.

Part (c)

Put \(w=\sqrt{5ag}\). The incoming velocity is \(3w\) and the outgoing velocity of \(P\) is \(-w\). Perfect restitution gives \(v_Q-(-w)=3w\), so \(v_Q=2w\). Momentum gives \(3mw=-mw+km(2w)\), and therefore \(k=2\).

original.title: A horizontal peg and a new circular path
original.stem_html: A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Its initial position \(A\) is above and to the right of \(O\), with \(OA\) at an acute angle \(\alpha\) to the upward vertical. It is projected tangentially clockwise with speed \(\sqrt{ag}\). A small smooth peg \(B\) is \(a/4\) horizontally to the left of \(O\). When the string first becomes horizontal to the left, it catches the peg; the particle then moves on a circle centred at \(B\). On its first ascent in this smaller circle it reaches \(C\), above and to the left of \(B\), where the radius makes an angle \(\gamma\) with the upward vertical and \(\cos\gamma=3/5\). The tension at \(C\) equals that at the initial point \(A\).
original.question_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Its initial position \(A\) is above and to the right of \(O\), with \(OA\) at an acute angle \(\alpha\) to the upward vertical. It is projected tangentially clockwise with speed \(\sqrt{ag}\). A small smooth peg \(B\) is \(a/4\) horizontally to the left of \(O\). When the string first becomes horizontal to the left, it catches the peg; the particle then moves on a circle centred at \(B\). On its first ascent in this smaller circle it reaches \(C\), above and to the left of \(B\), where the radius makes an angle \(\gamma\) with the upward vertical and \(\cos\gamma=3/5\). The tension at \(C\) equals that at the initial point \(A\).

(a) [3]

Find the speed squared when the string first catches the peg.

(b) [6]

Find \(\cos\alpha\).

(c) [3]

Check that C is reached before the string becomes slack in the smaller circle.
original.hint_html: Use a new radius and a new centre after the peg is caught; do not change the speed discontinuously.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(v_0^2=ag(1+2\cos\alpha)\).

(b)

\(\cos\alpha=2/5\).

(c)

In the smaller circle slackening occurs at cosine \(4/5\), after C.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The catch point is \((-a,0)\), whereas \(A\) has height \(a\cos\alpha\). The string tension does no work on the arc. Energy gives \[\frac12mv_0^2=\frac12mag+mga\cos\alpha,\] so \(v_0^2=ag(1+2\cos\alpha)\). The tangent is vertical at the catch, for both circles, so the speed is continuous there.

Part (b)

Put \(c=\cos\alpha\). At \(A\), \(T_A=mg(1-c)\). After catching the peg the effective radius is \(r=3a/4\). The point \(C\) is \((3a/4)(3/5)=9a/20\) above the catch level, so \[\frac{v_C^2}{ag}=1+2c-\frac9{10}.\] At \(C\), \(T_C+3mg/5=mv_C^2/(3a/4)\). Therefore \[\frac{T_C}{mg}=\frac43(1+2c)-\frac95.\] Equate this to \(1-c\): \((11/3)c=22/15\), giving \(c=2/5\). Both tensions are then \(3mg/5\).

Part (c)

With \(c=2/5\), the catch speed squared is \(9ag/5\). At a point whose radius from \(B\) has upward cosine \(z\), the tension is \[\frac{T}{mg}=\frac{9ag/5}{(3a/4)g}-3z=\frac{12}{5}-3z.\] It is zero at \(z=4/5\). During the first ascent \(z\) increases from zero; \(C\) has \(z=3/5\lt 4/5\). Its speed squared is \(9ag/10\gt 0\), so it is reached with positive tension.

It starts below and to the right of \(O\), with the string at an acute angle \(\theta\) to the downward vertical. It is projected tangentially downwards with speed \(\frac12\sqrt{3ag}\). At the lowest point the string catches a small smooth peg \(A\), situated \(a/2\) vertically below \(O\). It then rises in a circle about \(A\). The string first becomes slack when the new radius makes angle \(\theta\) with the upward vertical through \(A\).

(a) [5]

Find \(\cos\theta\).

(b) [3]

Find the ratio of the tensions immediately before and immediately after the string catches the peg.

(c) [2]

Find the speed when the string becomes slack.
original.hint_html: The force can change abruptly at the peg even though the speed does not.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\). The original starting height relative to \(O\) is \(-ac\). At the bottom the speed squared is \(ag(3/4+2(1-c))=ag(11/4-2c)\). The new radius is \(a/2\). At release the rise from the common lowest point is \((a/2)(1+c)\), so \[v_L^2=ag(11/4-2c)-ag(1+c)=ag(7/4-3c).\] Zero tension in the smaller circle gives \(v_L^2=(ag/2)c\). Equating yields \(7/4=(7/2)c\), and therefore \(c=1/2\).

Part (b)

At the catch, \(v^2=ag(11/4-1)=7ag/4\). The speed is unchanged but the radius halves. Thus \[T_-=mg+\frac{mv^2}{a}=\frac{11}{4}mg,\qquad T_+=mg+\frac{mv^2}{a/2}=\frac92mg.\] Their ratio is \(11:18\).

Part (c)

At zero tension, \(v_L^2=(ag/2)\cos\theta=ag/4\). Hence \(v_L=\sqrt{ag}/2\). This is positive, and tension decreases from \(9mg/2\) to zero on the specified ascent, so the first loss condition is valid.

When the rod has turned through \(60^\circ\), the speed of \(P\) is \(3\sqrt{ag/2}\). At this latter instant both portions of the rod are in tension and these two tensions are equal. The rod has negligible mass; include the kinetic energy of both particles.

(a) [2]

Express the speed of Q at the latter instant in terms of x, a and g.

(b) [5]

Find x.

(c) [4]

Find u.
original.hint_html: A light rigid rod can push as well as pull. Use the energies of the two particles, not a moment of inertia of a massive rod.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The two particles have the same instantaneous angular speed. Thus \(v_Q/x=v_P/(4a-x)\), so \(v_Q=3x\sqrt{ag/2}/(4a-x)\).

Part (b)

Put \(p=4a-x\). At \(60^\circ\), \(P\) is above the centre and \(Q\) is below it. The two inward equations are \[T_P+\frac12mg=\frac{m(9ag/2)}p,\qquad T_Q-\frac12mg=\frac{m(9ag/2)x}{p^2}.\] Using \(T_P=T_Q\) gives \((9a/2)(p-x)=p^2\). Write \(z=x/a\), so \((9/2)(4-2z)=(4-z)^2\). Hence \(z^2+z-2=0\), giving \(z=1\) or \(-2\). Only \(z=1\) lies in the allowed interval. Thus \(x=a\), and both tensions equal \(mg\gt 0\).

Part (c)

Now \(OP=3a\) and \(OQ=a\), so \(v_Q=v_P/3\) at all instants. During the turn, \(P\) falls by \(3a/2\) while \(Q\) rises by \(a/2\); the net potential-energy loss is \(mga\). Thus \[\frac12m\left(\frac{9ag}{2}+\frac{ag}{2}\right)-\frac12m\left(u^2+\frac{u^2}{9}\right)=mga.\] This gives \(5u^2/9=3ag/2\), hence \(u^2=27ag/10\). Initially the force in \(OP\) is compressive, of magnitude \(mg/10\); a rigid rod can supply this, unlike a string. No moment-of-inertia formula is required.
